DOCUMENT:
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate" -- Table 1 gives the pilot participation rate as 57% overall (66% houses, 21% flats); the projection applies a '64%' pilot participation rate. (64% x 52,000 x 1.9 kg x 52 = about 3,290 t; at 57% it would be about 2,930 t.)
2. [misread_evidence] at: "Participation was broadly similar across housing types" -- Table 1 shows participation of 66% in houses but only 21% in flats, a very large difference. The claim misreads the table, and the conclusion that a uniform service needs no separate approach for flats rests on it.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage." -- The saving assumes all projected tonnage (about 3,290 t) goes to Brookfield at £38/t, but the document states Brookfield can take only 1,800 t a year until 2029 and the next plant is 46 miles away. The excess tonnage's treatment and haulage cost is never addressed, though the 'fully funded' conclusion depends on it.

REVIEW:
## What the study argues

The study recommends a district-wide weekly food waste service from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot with 4,000 households. Its case has three parts:

- **Participation:** strong, and similar in houses and flats, so one uniform service will work.
- **Tonnage and savings:** about 3,290 tonnes a year, all treated at Brookfield, saving £74 per tonne.
- **Funding:** a net cost of about £490,000, covered by a £520,000 new-burdens allocation.

I checked each figure against Tables 1 and 2 and Section 4. The arithmetic within each table is correct. But three of the study's central conclusions are contradicted by its own figures:

- participation is not similar across housing types
- the 64% participation rate used for the projection matches nothing in the pilot
- Brookfield can take only about 60% of the projected tonnage

On corrected figures, the "fully funded" conclusion does not hold.

## 1. Participation in flats was a third of the rate in houses

Table 1 shows 66% participation in houses and **21% in flats**. Section 2's statement that "participation was broadly similar across housing types" is not what the table shows. The recommendation of a uniform service with no separate approach for flats rests on that misreading.

A 23-litre outdoor caddy suits houses with a front path. Flats typically need communal bins, bin-store signage and liaison with managing agents. The pilot suggests the uniform approach works for houses and largely fails in flats. A flats-specific approach should be designed and costed before roll-out.

## 2. The projection uses a participation rate the pilot didn't produce

Section 3 applies "the pilot's 64% participation rate". The pilot's overall rate was **57%**. 64% doesn't correspond to any figure in Table 1.

The pilot happens to have the same housing mix as the district (20% flats), so its overall results can be scaled directly:

| | Houses | Flats | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| District households | 41,600 | 10,400 | 52,000 |
| Participation (pilot) | 66% | 21% | 57% |
| kg per participating household per week | 1.9 | 1.4 | about 1.86 |
| **Tonnes per year** | about 2,713 | about 159 | **about 2,870** |

That is about 13% below the study's 3,290 tonnes. The disposal saving falls accordingly, from £243,000 to about **£212,000**.

Two further points could push the figure lower:

- **Season and novelty:** January to June is one half of the year, and pilot participation often declines once the service is no longer new. A full-year view would settle this.
- **Liners:** pilot households received liners, but roll-out households get a three-month supply. If liners stop after that, participation may drop. The study should say whether the £88,000 line covers liners on an ongoing basis.

## 3. Brookfield can take only 1,800 tonnes a year until 2029

Section 4 states this limit, but the savings calculation ignores it. Both the study's projection and the corrected one exceed it:

- Study's projection: 3,290 tonnes, which is **about 1,490 tonnes over**
- Corrected projection: about 2,870 tonnes, which is **about 1,070 tonnes over**

The surplus would have to go to the next plant, 46 miles away. Its gate fee is not stated, and the extra haulage would add vehicle, crew and fuel time.

"Treatment is local" is therefore true for about 1,800 tonnes. The saving of £74 per tonne is supported only up to that volume, worth about **£133,000**. The saving on the remaining tonnage is unknown until the second plant's gate fee and the haulage cost are priced.

The expansion is described as "planned" for 2029. Until there is a contract, it is a hope rather than capacity the Council can rely on.

## 4. On corrected figures, the service is not fully funded

The cost table itself is accurate:

- Vehicles: 6 × £165,000 ÷ 7 years = £141,400
- Crews: 12 operatives × £34,000 = £408,000
- Total: £733,400

What changes is the saving set against it:

| Scenario | Disposal saving | Net cost | Compared with £520,000 provisional allocation |
|---|---|---|---|
| As stated (3,290 t, all at Brookfield) | £243,000 | £490,400 | £29,600 headroom |
| Corrected tonnage (2,870 t, all at Brookfield) | £212,400 | £521,000 | **About £1,000 short** |
| Corrected tonnage, Brookfield capped at 1,800 t, surplus not yet costed | £133,200 + unknown | Up to £600,200 | **Up to about £80,000 short** |

The last row is a ceiling, not an estimate. The surplus tonnage would still save something: the difference between £112 per tonne for incineration and the far plant's gate fee plus haulage.

Even on the study's own figures, the headroom was only £30,000, and the allocation is described as provisional. The table also leaves out several costs:

- **Up-front capital:** buying the vehicles requires about £990,000 in 2026–27. The study doesn't say whether new-burdens funding covers capital or only revenue.
- **Cover:** there is no spare vehicle, and no crew cover for leave and sickness.
- **Running costs:** supervision, and the phone line and web page listed in Section 6.

## 5. The timetable has no slack

Working back from the vehicle lead time is the right approach. But vehicles are due to arrive in March 2027, with crews trained on them in March and collections starting on 5 April. A late vehicle delivery delays the launch directly. The plan should state a fallback, such as hired vehicles.

The Brookfield contract and any second-plant arrangement also need to be in place by April. Section 6 doesn't mention either.

**Check the statutory date.** As I understand the Simpler Recycling rules, most English councils were required to start weekly household food waste collections by 31 March 2026, with later dates only under transitional arrangements. If that is right, an April 2027 start needs Thornbury to have such an arrangement. Confirm this against the regulations or Defra guidance. If Thornbury has no transitional date, the paper should acknowledge that the service will start late.

## 6. What holds up

- **Participation in houses (66%)** is solid evidence that the service works there.
- **Contamination under 2%**, measured at the treatment plant, is a good result.
- **Satisfaction (81%)** is encouraging. The survey response rate isn't given, though, and respondents are likely to be skewed towards participants.
- **The cost arithmetic** and the £74 per tonne saving are correct, within Brookfield's capacity.

## 7. Settled and open

**Settled by the study's own figures:**
- Participation in flats is 21% against 66% in houses.
- The pilot's overall participation was 57%, not 64%.
- Projected tonnage is about 2,870 tonnes, not 3,290.
- Brookfield's contracted capacity covers about 1,800 tonnes.
- On corrected tonnage, the net cost slightly exceeds the provisional allocation, even if all tonnage went to Brookfield.

**Open:**

| Question | What would settle it |
|---|---|
| Cost of treating about 1,070 tonnes above Brookfield's capacity | A quoted gate fee from the 46-mile plant, plus costed haulage |
| Whether new-burdens funding covers capital, and what the final allocation will be | Written confirmation from government |
| What service for flats would work, and at what cost | A costed design, with communal bins and agent liaison, ideally trialled briefly |
| Participation over a full year without free liners | Continued monitoring of the pilot wards through the second half of 2026 |
| Whether the April 2027 start is compliant | The regulations or Defra guidance, and any transitional arrangement for Thornbury |

## Recommendation

Approve the vehicle order, since the lead time drives the whole timetable and the service is required regardless. Don't yet approve the roll-out as "fully funded". Ask for a revised paper that:

1. Uses 57% participation, or rates by housing type, and the corrected tonnage of about 2,870 tonnes.
2. Costs treatment of the tonnage above Brookfield's 1,800-tonne cap.
3. Designs and costs a separate approach for flats.
4. Adds capital funding, vehicle and crew cover, and supervision costs.
5. Confirms the new-burdens terms and the statutory start date.

The service may still be affordable, and for houses the pilot is good evidence that it will work. But the Council should approve it on the corrected figures, not on a 64% participation rate and unlimited capacity at £38 per tonne.
